Model system · Medicago sativa
01 / 04 · Canopy

Alfalfa, above ground.

This is the plant in all of my experiments. The light and water treatments are applied up here, at the leaves.

02 / 04 · Soil line

The soil line.

A plant under stress changes what its roots release into the soil. That is how a treatment applied to the leaves ends up reaching the bacteria.

03 / 04 · Rhizosphere

The rhizosphere.

The few millimetres of soil around each root hold a bacterial community that the root feeds and shapes. Which species persist under combined stress, and what they do there, is the main question of my PhD.

04 / 04 · Nodules

Root nodules.

Alfalfa hosts Sinorhizobium meliloti in nodules on its roots, where the bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant. Active nodules are pink from leghemoglobin. This is the pairing the Phytobiome model is built around.

Research

My PhD project looks at how environmental conditions, on their own and in combination, change which bacteria live around plant roots and what those bacteria do. I work with alfalfa (Medicago sativa) in the Microbiome Manipulation Lab, and the two factors I spend most of my time on are light and water.

Most microbiome studies change one condition at a time. In a field, a plant is often short of water and light in the same week. I want to know whether the bacterial community responds to both together in a way you could have predicted from the single-factor experiments, or not. That is the question my experiments are set up to answer.

Combined stressors

Light and water treatments applied at the same time, with the bacterial community sampled across all the combinations.

Plant–bacteria signalling

What a stressed plant releases from its roots, and how the bacteria around them respond to it.

Microbiome manipulation

Passaging soil communities over repeated generations to select for a function, then testing whether it actually holds.

Phytobiome

Active build

Phytobiome is a browser simulation of an alfalfa plant and its microbiome. You set sixteen environmental variables and pick from thirteen organisms, and the plant grows, wilts, flowers or dies depending on what you gave it. The whole thing is one HTML file with no server behind it.

I built it with Arvin Shojaei-Fard, a software engineer and data analyst. The plant is paired with its real symbiont, Sinorhizobium meliloti. Every variable has a real unit, and every symptom the plant shows is linked to the paper it was taken from.

Research positions

03/2024 – 08/2024
Algae Biotechnology — Master's thesis
GEPEA lab & AlgoSolis platform, Nantes University, Saint-Nazaire, France

Scaled up and tuned conditions for a calcite-based protective coating grown on concrete by microalgae, intended to protect wind turbines in a marine environment. Tested multiple regimes to enhance biofilm formation and biomineralization, and showed enhanced calcite deposition by microalgae over abiotic spontaneous precipitation.

09/2023 – 03/2024
Algae Biorefinery project
Institute of Natural Materials Technology, TU Dresden, Germany

Identified the most favourable conditions for pigment production, including astaxanthin, under green, white, blue and red light spectra. Continuous microalgae cultivation in a CellDeg photobioreactor, with lipid and pigment extraction, dry biomass and spectrophotometry. Project: “Analysis of the macromolecular composition of microalgae as a function of spectral light condition.”
